questions.question: The density of air at $T = 0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($273\ \mathrm{K}$) and $P = 1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ is $\rho_0 = 1.29\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$. Find the density at $T = 100^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($373\ \mathrm{K}$) at the same pressure.
questions.answer:
At constant pressure, from $PV = nRT$ and $\rho = m/V = nM/V$:

$\rho = \dfrac{PM}{RT}$, so $\rho \propto 1/T$ at constant $P$.

$\rho_{100} = \rho_0 \times \dfrac{T_0}{T_{100}} = 1.29 \times \dfrac{273}{373} = 1.29 \times 0.732 \approx 0.944\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$

Hot air is less dense — which is why hot air rises (buoyancy).

questions.question: Derive the formula $\rho = PM/(RT)$ for the density of an ideal gas, where $M$ is the molar mass.
questions.answer:
Start with the ideal gas law: $PV = nRT$

The mass of gas: $m = nM$ (where $M$ is molar mass in kg/mol)

Density: $\rho = m/V = nM/V$

From ideal gas law: $n/V = P/(RT)$

Therefore:

$$\rho = \frac{nM}{V} = \frac{PM}{RT}$$

At fixed $P$ and $M$: $\rho \propto 1/T$ (density decreases with temperature)

At fixed $T$ and $M$: $\rho \propto P$ (density increases with pressure)

questions.question: A sealed container holds air (molar mass $M = 0.029\ \mathrm{kg/mol}$) at $T = 300\ \mathrm{K}$ and $P = 1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Find: (a) the density, (b) the temperature at which density would be halved (at same pressure).

A gas has density $\rho_1 = 2.0\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ at $T_1 = 20^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $P_1 = 2.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$. It is heated to $T_2 = 80^\circ\mathrm{C}$ while pressure drops to $P_2 = 1.5\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Find the new density $\rho_2$.

Two identical balloons are filled with the same mass of gas. Balloon A is at $T_A = 300\ \mathrm{K}$ and Balloon B is at $T_B = 400\ \mathrm{K}$, both at atmospheric pressure $P = 1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Find the ratio of their volumes $V_B/V_A$.
questions.answer:
Same mass of gas $\Rightarrow$ same number of moles $n$, same $P$.

From $PV = nRT$: at constant $n$ and $P$, $V \propto T$

$\dfrac{V_B}{V_A} = \dfrac{T_B}{T_A} = \dfrac{400}{300} = \dfrac{4}{3}$

Balloon B has 4/3 the volume of Balloon A.

**Density check:** $\rho = m/V = m/(nRT/P) \propto 1/T$

$\rho_B/\rho_A = T_A/T_B = 3/4$ — the hot balloon has lower density.

questions.question: The density of nitrogen ($M = 0.028\ \mathrm{kg/mol}$) at $T = 0^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $P_0 = 1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$ is $\rho_0$. Find $\rho_0$, and then find the density at $27^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $2.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

A weather balloon at ground level contains helium ($M = 0.004\ \mathrm{kg/mol}$) at $T = 20^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $P = 1.01\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Find: (a) the density of helium, (b) the density of surrounding air ($M_\mathrm{air} = 0.029\ \mathrm{kg/mol}$) at the same conditions, (c) the buoyancy force on a $10\ \mathrm{m^3}$ balloon.
At what temperature must oxygen ($M = 0.032\ \mathrm{kg/mol}$) be heated, at constant pressure, so that its density equals $\rho_0/4$ (one-quarter of its initial density at $T_0 = 300\ \mathrm{K}$)?
questions.answer:
At constant pressure: $\rho \propto 1/T$

$\dfrac{\rho}{\rho_0} = \dfrac{T_0}{T}$

$\dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{300}{T}$

$T = 4 \times 300 = 1200\ \mathrm{K} = 927^\circ\mathrm{C}$

Oxygen must be heated to $1200\ \mathrm{K}$ for its density to be one-quarter of its $300\ \mathrm{K}$ value.

questions.question: A container of volume $V = 0.5\ \mathrm{m^3}$ holds oxygen ($M = 0.032\ \mathrm{kg/mol}$) at $T = 300\ \mathrm{K}$ and $P = 1.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Find: (a) the number of moles, (b) the mass, (c) the density.

The relative density of a gas compared to air is $d = M_{\text{gas}}/M_{\text{air}}$. Gas A has $d = 2$ (twice as heavy as air, same conditions). How does its density compare to air, and at what temperature (in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$) must air be heated (at the same pressure) to have the same density as gas A at $0^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
questions.answer:
At the same $T$ and $P$: $\rho = PM/(RT)$, so $\rho \propto M$.

$\rho_{\text{gas A}} = 2\rho_{\text{air}}$ at the same conditions.

At $T_0 = 273\ \mathrm{K}$ (0°C), $\rho_{\text{gas A}} = 2 \times 1.29 = 2.58\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$

For air to reach this density at the same pressure: $\rho_{\text{air}}(T) = 2\rho_{\text{air}}(273)$

$\dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{2}{273}$... Wait, $\rho \propto 1/T$, so to have **twice** the density, $T$ must be **halved**:

Actually: $\rho \propto 1/T$. For $\rho$ to double, $T$ must halve. But we want air density = gas A density at $0^\circ$C, i.e., $\rho_{\text{air}}(T) = 2\rho_{\text{air}}(273)$

$T = 273/2 = 136.5\ \mathrm{K} = -136.5^\circ\mathrm{C}$

Air must be cooled (not heated) to $-136.5^\circ\mathrm{C}$ — confirming that heavy gas A is denser than air at any temperature above absolute zero.
